title: Redundancy & Failover
subtitle: Watch a single-path system break, then add spare parts until one failure no longer takes the site down.
learn: How to spot a single point of failure (SPOF) in a request path
Why chained components multiply availability down, and parallel ones multiply failure odds down
The difference between active-active and active-passive redundancy
How health checks and failover work, and what they cost in time and data
Why redundancy fails when the copies share a fate

steps.title: One machine, one bad day
steps.body: Picture an online shop running on one app server. Availability is the share of time it works. This server is up 99.9% of the time, called "three nines" (each extra nine cuts allowed downtime tenfold). That sounds great, but the missing 0.1% of a year is about 526 minutes, nearly 9 hours when nobody can buy anything. Disks fill, hardware dies and bad releases ship. So how do you keep serving when one part breaks?
steps.idea: Every machine will fail eventually. The design question is what users see when it does.
steps.caption: One server, 99.9% available, about 526 minutes of downtime a year.

steps.title: Find the single points of failure
steps.body: Follow one request through the diagram. It passes a load balancer (it spreads traffic across servers), one app server, then one database. Each is a single point of failure (SPOF): if it dies, the request fails. All three must work at the same time, called "in series", so you multiply their availability. 0.9999 x 0.999 x 0.999 is about 99.79%, roughly 1,100 minutes a year. A chain is always less reliable than its weakest link.
steps.idea: In a chain, availabilities multiply, so the whole is always worse than its worst part.
steps.caption: One request crosses three parts in a row. Each one is a SPOF.

steps.title: Add a spare in parallel
steps.body: We add a second app server, B, beside A, and the balancer can now send requests to either. The app layer fails only when both are down at once. If each is down 0.1% of the time and they fail independently (one failing says nothing about the other), both are down 0.001 x 0.001 = 0.000001 of the time. That layer is 99.9999% available. The whole system rises to about 99.89%, but the single database (99.9%) is now the weakest part.
steps.idea: Side by side, you multiply failure odds together, which shrinks them fast. This only helps the layer you duplicated.
steps.caption: The balancer can now pick either of two servers.

steps.title: Active-active: all copies work
steps.body: The animation splits 100 requests a second across both servers, 50 each. This is active-active: every copy works all the time, so when one dies the balancer just stops sending it traffic. The catch is spare room. If each server runs at 70% load and one dies, the survivor must take 140% and falls over too. With two servers, keep each under 50% load. With four, up to 75% each is safe. Planning so the survivors can carry everything is called N+1.
steps.idea: Active-active needs spare capacity: after a failure, the remaining copies must absorb the whole load.
steps.caption: 100 req/s is split 50/50 across both servers.

steps.title: Detect the failure and route around it
steps.body: App server A crashes. The health checker (a small service that pings each server) sends probes (tiny test requests) and gets no reply from A. It probes every 5 seconds and declares A unhealthy after 3 misses in a row, so about 15 seconds pass while users still hit a dead server. Then the balancer is told, stops using A and sends all traffic to B, which answers 200 OK (the standard success reply). Faster probes shorten the gap but risk false alarms from one slow reply.
steps.idea: Failover means detecting the failure, then rerouting. Detection time is downtime you must plan for.
steps.caption: Probes to A fail, the balancer is told, and traffic shifts to B.

steps.title: Active-passive for stateful parts
steps.body: Databases are harder to copy than app servers because they hold data, and two copies that both accept writes would disagree. The usual answer is active-passive: one primary takes all writes and streams every change (the moving "change log") to a standby that only follows. The copying is often asynchronous, meaning the primary does not wait for the standby, so the standby can lag by milliseconds to seconds. That lag is the data you could lose in a crash. (Server A is repaired and back in rotation.)
steps.idea: Active-passive keeps one writer to avoid conflicts. Asynchronous copying is fast but can lose the last few writes.
steps.caption: Apps write to the primary, which streams changes to an idle standby.

steps.title: Failing over the database
steps.body: Now the primary dies. The standby sees the change stream stop, and the health checker confirms the primary is silent. Before promoting the standby, the old primary must be fenced off (cut off from network and storage). Otherwise a half-alive old primary and the new one could both accept writes, called split-brain. Then the standby is promoted (made the new primary) and the apps send writes to it. Assume about 30 seconds in total; real systems range from seconds to a couple of minutes. Writes in that window fail or queue, and changes not yet copied may be lost. The whole system now sits near 99.99%, about 55 minutes a year, mostly from the single balancer.
steps.idea: Stateful failover is slower and can lose recent writes, so measure it instead of assuming it is instant.
steps.caption: Primary fails, the standby is promoted, and apps move their writes over.

steps.title: The spare you forgot
steps.body: What is still single? The load balancer and the health checker. In the animation, users reach a dead balancer and fail. The balancer alone causes about 53 of those 55 minutes a year (99.99%). Fix it with two balancers sharing a floating IP (an address that jumps to whichever balancer is alive). DNS (answers may be cached for minutes) or anycast (many sites announce one address and the network sends users to a live one) also work. Add checkers in several places too. That leaves about 1 minute a year, mostly switch-over time. Add 4 database failovers a year at 30 s, which is 2 minutes. Total: about 3 minutes.
steps.idea: Every layer you forget is still a SPOF. Redundancy is only as good as its least-duplicated part.
steps.caption: The balancer fails for users. A second balancer and checker would fix it (not drawn).

steps.title: When copies share a fate
steps.body: The parallel math assumed independent failures. Here both servers sit on one rack, share one power feed and just received the same buggy release. One cause kills both at once, and the checker gets no reply from either. The pair now acts like one server. Even with a perfect balancer and database, the app layer is only 99.9%, so the system falls back to about 99.9% (roughly 530 minutes a year). Fix this by spreading copies across racks and availability zones (isolated data-centre groups within a region), staggering deploys, and trying each new version on a canary (a small first slice of traffic).
steps.idea: Redundancy only helps when failures are independent. Correlated failures make two copies behave like one.
steps.caption: One shared cause takes down both servers at once.

steps.title: Spare parts, honestly counted
steps.body: Remove SPOFs layer by layer: servers, database, balancer, even the checker. In a chain, availability multiplies down. Side by side, failure odds multiply down. Stateless tiers (no stored data) are easy to run active-active. Stateful ones usually use one writer plus a standby, unless the datastore is built for multiple writers. Count detection and promotion time as downtime, keep spare capacity, and spread copies so one cause cannot hit them all. A later lesson on multi-region extends these ideas.
steps.idea: Remove SPOFs in every layer, keep failures independent, and budget for the failover itself.
steps.caption: Redundant at every layer and spread across failure domains.

quiz.q: A request needs service X and service Y in series. Each is 99% available and they fail independently. Roughly what is the combined availability?
quiz.why: In series you multiply: 0.99 x 0.99 = 0.9801, about 98%. The chain is worse than either part alone.

quiz.q: Two identical servers, each 99% available and failing independently, sit in parallel behind a perfect balancer. What is the best estimate for the pair?
quiz.why: The pair is down only when both are down: 0.01 x 0.01 = 0.0001, so 99.99%. This holds only if failures are truly independent.

quiz.q: Two active-active servers each run at 65% of capacity. One crashes. What most likely happens?
options: Nothing, since the other server was healthy
The survivor needs about 130% of capacity and overloads
The load balancer adds a server automatically
Latency halves because there is less to coordinate
quiz.why: The survivor inherits all the traffic, 65% + 65% = 130% of one server. Active-active needs headroom so survivors can carry the full load.

quiz.q: Why can promoting a database standby lose data even though it worked as designed?
options: The load balancer drops write requests
Promotion always wipes the new primary
Asynchronous replication may not have delivered the primary's last few changes
quiz.why: With asynchronous replication the primary acknowledges writes before the standby has them, so a crash can lose the lag window. Synchronous replication avoids that at the cost of slower writes.

quiz.q: You run two app servers in the same rack, deploying the same new build to both at once. Why is your 'parallel' math misleading?
options: The failures are correlated, so one cause can take both down together
Racks do not support load balancing
The math only works for databases
quiz.why: Multiplying failure probabilities requires independence. A shared rack, power feed or bad release breaks that assumption, so the pair acts like one.

cheatsheet.def: Single point of failure: any component whose failure stops the whole service because nothing can replace it.
Series (all parts must work): multiply availabilities, 0.999 x 0.999 = 0.998. Parallel (any one suffices): 1 - (1 - a)^n, so two 99% copies give 99.99% if independent.
Two nodes both believe they are the primary and accept conflicting writes. Prevent it with fencing of the old primary and a quorum or consensus vote before promotion.
99.9% allows about 526 min/year of downtime; 99.99% about 53 min; 99.999% about 5 min.
All copies serve traffic at once. Failover is just removal from rotation, but spare capacity (N+1) is needed.
One copy serves while a standby follows. Suits stateful systems with a single writer; failover needs a promotion step.
A probe such as an HTTP /health call every few seconds. Detection time is roughly interval x failures to mark unhealthy.
A group that can fail together (rack, power feed, zone, release). Spread copies across domains so failures stay independent.
